summary: This experimental RFC describes a pre-shared key authentication method for IKE. It resists dictionary attacks and stays secure even if the shared key is weak, which ordinary pre-shared key authentication does not.

plainLanguage.summary: A secret password can be guessed if it is simple. This is a way to prove you know it without giving enough clues for someone to guess.

what is secure psk authentication for ike

what is the dragonfly key exchange
subtitle: Authentication method for IKE resistant to dictionary attacks with weak passwords

tldr.problem: The standard IKEv2 pre-shared key authentication method is vulnerable to dictionary attacks and only provides security with very long, random keys. Human-memorable passwords are too weak to be secure with it.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC defines a zero-knowledge-proof-based authentication method called Dragonfly that computes a secret group element from the shared password and uses ephemeral key exchange to prove knowledge of the password, limiting attackers to one guess per active attack.
tldr.outcome: The method allows users to authenticate with weak passwords like four-character strings while remaining secure against dictionary attacks, making IKE more practical for remote access VPNs and other scenarios with human-chosen credentials.

facts.label: Supported groups
facts.value: MODP and ECP (not characteristic-two elliptic curves)

today: RFC 6617 is an experimental specification providing secure password authentication for IKEv2. The Dragonfly algorithm has also been adopted in other contexts, including 802.11 SAE (Simultaneous Authentication of Equals) for wireless networks. The RFC has not been updated or obsoleted.

sections.title: Dictionary Attack Resistance for Passwords
sections.content:
The IKEv2 standard allows authentication with pre-shared keys (PSKs), but the method is susceptible to dictionary attacks. The RFC recommends PSKs containing as much entropy as the encryption keys they authenticate—over 100 characters for non-hexadecimal keys—which is impractical for users to enter. Weak human-memorable passwords provide no security with the standard method.

This RFC specifies Secure PSK Authentication, a method based on zero-knowledge proofs that achieves dictionary attack resistance: an attacker can make only one guess at the password per active attack, regardless of password weakness. The method is based on the Dragonfly key exchange algorithm, which has also been deployed in 802.11 wireless networks and as an EAP method.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of just checking if the password is right, this method proves you know the password without letting attackers guess many times. Even a simple password becomes secure because an attacker only gets one try.

sections.title: Discrete Logarithm Cryptography
sections.content:
The authentication method uses discrete logarithm cryptography: either finite field cryptography (MODP groups, which use modular exponentiation) or elliptic curve cryptography (ECP groups). These are the same groups already negotiated in IKE.

The protocol defines operations on group elements: scalar-op (multiplying a group element by a scalar to produce another element), element-op (combining two elements), and inverse-op (finding an element that combines with the first to produce the identity). For MODP groups, scalar-op is exponentiation; for ECP groups, it is point multiplication on an elliptic curve.
sections.plainLanguage: The math uses special number tricks where you can compute Y = G^x but it is very hard to find x if you know G and Y. This is the hard problem that keeps the authentication secure.

sections.title: The Secure PSK Authentication Exchange
sections.content:
Both peers first derive a Secret Key Element (SKE) from the shared password using a hunting-and-pecking technique. The password is passed to a pseudo-random function with a counter, repeatedly until the result is a valid element in the negotiated group. This computation is deterministic from the password, so both peers derive the same SKE.

Next, each peer generates a Commit payload containing a scalar and an element, derived from ephemeral random values and the SKE. The peers exchange Commit payloads and use them to derive a shared secret, proving knowledge of the password. The Commit payload binds the sender to a single guess of the password; an attacker forging a Commit payload gets only one guess, because the subsequent AUTH payload would not verify unless that guess was correct.
sections.plainLanguage: Both sides compute a magic number from the shared password. Then they prove to each other they computed the same number by sending secret messages that only make sense if they have the same magic number.

sections.title: Password Preprocessing and Obfuscation
sections.content:
If the pre-shared key is a human-readable password or passphrase, it must be preprocessed before use. The password is first processed according to the SASLprep profile to remove internationalization ambiguities and produce a UTF-8 string. Next, the processed password is obfuscated by computing HMAC-SHA256 using the password as the key and the fixed string IKE Secure PSK Authentication as the data.

If the PSK is already a hexadecimal or binary string, it is used directly without preprocessing. Devices storing passwords should preprocess them before storage to reduce exposure in case of server compromise.
sections.plainLanguage: Regular passwords are cleaned up and mixed up using a math function so that even if someone steals the stored password, they cannot directly use it.

sections.title: Security Against Dictionary Attacks
sections.content:
The protocol achieves dictionary attack resistance because an attacker must launch an active attack, impersonating one side of the exchange and sending a forged Commit payload. By committing to a Commit payload before seeing the peer's AUTH payload, the attacker locks in one specific guess of the password. If that guess is wrong, the computed AUTH payload will not match, and no amount of subsequent guessing will help.

The security parameter k ensures that the hunting-and-pecking loop runs at least k iterations regardless of when SKE is found, preventing side-channel attacks that could leak information about the password length from the number of iterations.
sections.plainLanguage: An attacker has to pick a password guess and prove they know it before they see any proof from the real person. If they guess wrong, they cannot just try again.
